nameStory: The Lilypad Clubtail gets its name from its favorite perching spots — the broad, flat leaves of water lilies floating on pond surfaces. Like all clubtails, it has a distinctive swollen tip at the end of its abdomen that looks like a tiny club. This combination of habitat preference and body shape makes the name perfectly descriptive!
description: The Lilypad Clubtail is a medium-sized dragonfly that's perfectly at home around quiet ponds and slow-moving waters. These sleek hunters have the typical clubtail build — a relatively slender body that widens noticeably at the tail end, creating that characteristic 'club' shape. Adults are strong fliers with clear wings and earth-toned bodies that help them blend in with their pond-side surroundings. You'll often spot them perched motionless on lily pads or other floating vegetation, waiting to dart out after small flying insects.

idTips.label: Club-shaped tail
idTips.description: The abdomen swells dramatically at the tip, creating an unmistakable club or paddle shape that's wider than the rest of the body

idTips.label: Lily pad perching
idTips.description: Often found resting horizontally on floating lily pads or other broad aquatic vegetation, wings held perpendicular to the body

idTips.label: Earth-toned coloring
idTips.description: Body shows muted browns and yellows with darker markings, helping it blend with dried vegetation and pond edges

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are transparent with fine dark veining and may show a slight amber tint at the base

idTips.label: Eyes well-separated
idTips.description: Unlike darners, the large compound eyes don't touch at the top of the head but are clearly separated

habitat: Look for Lilypad Clubtails around quiet ponds, slow backwaters, and marshy areas with abundant floating vegetation, especially water lilies and spatterdock. They prefer still or very slow-moving waters with muddy bottoms and emergent plants. You'll find them in lowland areas throughout New England, from small woodland ponds to larger marshy lakes.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their aquatic larval stage in late spring, but are not yet at peak numbers. Early emergers may be seen near breeding waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen perching on lily pads and hunting. This is the best time for identification and observation of their distinctive behaviors.
seasonality.fall: Adults become less active and harder to find as temperatures cool. Late-season individuals may still be spotted on warm, sunny days near their pond habitats.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity — they spend winter as larvae (nymphs) buried in pond mud, developing slowly until ready to emerge the following year.

funFact: Lilypad Clubtail larvae are ambush predators that bury themselves completely in pond mud with only their eyes and breathing tube exposed, then shoot out an extendable jaw like a harpoon to snatch passing prey — they can remain motionless in this buried position for weeks!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Unicorn Clubtail, which shares similar habitats and the distinctive clubbed tail. The key difference is that Unicorn Clubtails have a prominent horn-like projection on the face (hence the name), while Lilypad Clubtails have a smooth face profile. Memory trick: 'No horn, loves lily platforms for sitting on.'
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'furcifer' means 'fork-bearer,' referring to the forked appendages at the tip of the male's club-shaped tail. These are actually claspers used during mating and are an important identification feature for dragonfly experts.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Unicorn Clubtail, the Lilypad Clubtail lacks the distinctive horn-like facial projection and tends to perch more often on floating vegetation rather than shoreline perches. Both species share the characteristic swollen tail tip, but the Lilypad Clubtail's face appears smooth and rounded in profile, while the Unicorn Clubtail's face has that unmistakable forward-pointing bump.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The unicorn clubtail differs from its close relative, the lilypad clubtail, primarily in the male's facial features - unicorn clubtails have that distinctive horn-like projection while lilypad clubtails have a more rounded face.
